rationale: A wins because it treats the sponsor-funded study as a live grenade, not a brochure bullet. Its "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works" angle forces the proof questions that decide whether Calm should pitch science at all; B's "Calm funded a study of its own app" is competent but softer. B also steps on a factual rake with "Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly" - covered members are not users.
gaps_in_A: "demand for care exceeds clinician supply" is invented context. The update gives no clinician-supply fact, and A even refuses a similar crisis-frame later for lacking evidence.
"the primary outcome is self-reported" upgrades the supplied fact. The update says self-reported anxiety scores fell; it does not say that was the primary outcome.
"on the plan's dime" implies payer economics the update does not disclose. The safer claim is that members get Premium at no cost.

The category and insurer angles sit close together: "consumer wellness subscription crossing into covered-benefit status" and "three national carriers made a purchasing decision" need careful targeting so they do not become the same payer story twice.
gaps_in_B: "Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly" overclaims. The fact is 25 million covered members, not 25 million users.

The study angle is too polite for the risk. "funding structure... head-on" is good, but it misses pre-registration, conflict terms, publication control, and whether the 18% is between-group or within-group.
"A health or science reporter" and "consumer-health or benefits-trade reporter" are broad buckets. They need the sharper sub-beat definition A gives.
The next step skips the first safety gate: before pitching the study, Calm needs a fact-check on the trial design and the 18% claim, not just journalist matching.
